utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before the Prosecution will call its next witness, we first have to decide on the admissibility of the documents tendered during the testimony of Mr. Harding. But before doing so, I've one more question. In February, the major objection of the Defence was that the three documents, apart from the photographs, had been disclosed so late that they could not accept this late disclosure and that they were handicapped in the preparation of the cross-examination. At that time, there was also a question about a translation. Has a translation been provided and when has the translation been provided? Could you please, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The translations were given, I think, two or three days after the originals were given in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see Ms. Pilipovic nodding. That means that as we indicated already in February, that the main reason at that moment was not to admit these documents in evidence because there had not been enough time to prepare for cross-examination on these documents; and apart from that, they were not translated. As we already indicated at that time, this might change to the extent that if at a later stage there would have been enough time to prepare for cross-examination, if necessary, if the witness would have been recalled to be cross-examined, that the situation might then be different. Well, we are now in this different situation, approximately five weeks in between the first examination of the witness and the final opportunity for the Defence to cross-examine the witness, and the Chamber deems that this was enough. Therefore, the documents are admitted into evidence. Madam Registrar, we had three documents. Perhaps you could please repeat the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, they are admitted in evidence. The photographs yesterday, there were no objections any more from the part of the Defence already in February. I see that there are photocopies, coloured photocopies, available for all the parties, so I suggest that the coloured version of these photographs, that is P3662, is tendered and is admitted in evidence. Madam Registrar, then we had the map marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map marked by the witness, P3644.CH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And Defence map, D53.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also admitted in evidence. Having dealt with the documents, I think, Mr. Waespi or it's you, Mr. Mundis, who is going to examine the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, thank you for giving us the floor. Before the next witness enters the courtroom, the Defence would like to raise once again a problem regarding the documents that were disclosed to us. The reasons for which we objected to the three documents that have just been admitted was a reason of principle. The Defence, like others, no doubt, believes that the Rules of Procedure should be fully observed. We have -- we will hear a very important witness who was in charge of the Fire Brigade and who could testify about the relevant period during the war. Mr. President, we received yesterday documents in the form of a computer printout, the number of interventions carried out by that brigade in Sarajevo. I'm showing this because it is one page, and we have dozens of pages in this same format received a few days ago only or, rather, a few hours ago from the Prosecution. When I look at these documents, I note several things. First of all, on a single page, there is about a hundred items of information, and we received something of this thickness which means we will have several thousand items of information. On some of these documents, 436 problems of translation arise. The Prosecution has managed to transform a written document which is comparable to an epigraph, the contrary of epigraph. So in addition to these problems of translation, it was simply not possible for the Defence to examine all these documents in the few free hours that we have had after the Easter holidays. What I'm trying to say, that what the Defence could have done was to compare each of these pieces of information within the map of legitimate military targets which we're about to establish, and to be able to cross-examine this witness and say to him, "But in this school, wasn't there in reality the barracks of such and such a brigade?" "And in that warehouse, did it not contain trucks in the possession of the army," et cetera, et cetera? I don't know which Defence in the world could in a few hours perform this work. I'm your humble servant, but I cannot do it. I simply cannot. And if this international justice requires this of the Defence, I can take off my headphones and sit down because I have nothing more to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please respond, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Excel format spreadsheets to which Mr. Piletta-Zanin refers were disclosed to the Defence on a CD-Rom on the 26th of November, 2001. On January 2nd of the present year, we informed the Defence that -- via letter -- that these spreadsheets that were contained on this CD-Rom would most likely be introduced through the next witness. We then did take the additional step of printing out the spreadsheets for the benefit of the Defence, and that's the document to which Mr. Piletta-Zanin refers that was placed in their locker yesterday. However, I should again like to stress that they have had this information on a CD-Rom in electronic form since November 26th of last year. And my case manager informs me that they were actually placed in the Defence locker, the printouts of the information contained on the CD-Rom, on the 28th of March, which was immediately prior to the Easter holiday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give us some additional information? I'm just giving an example. If you'd use a telephone directory in evidence, that would not mean that you would check the correctness of every telephone number related to every person, not necessarily. It could also be used in order to establish that someone was listed in a telephone directory. Could you tell us a bit about how you intend to use these materials, because this might give us a better understanding of the problems the Defence might have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour raises another interesting point. The Prosecution has determined during the final proofing of this witness yesterday that we will not actually be tendering these documents into evidence, but they have been provided to the Defence so the Defence could use them as they see fit during cross-examination. But to briefly explain what these documents are, they are simple compilations of the Fire Brigade records with respect to what the witness will testify as to interventions, which simply means that any time the Fire Brigade was called, documents were made indicating where they went, what type of fire -- the address where they went, what type of fire or other intervention it was. A variety of statistics are then taken which are reflected on these spreadsheets, and then in a final column it indicates, or towards the right of the document, in a column it indicates an assessment based on the senior firefighter at the scene on whether the fire was intentionally set, whether it was due to negligence, whether it was due to an electrical short circuit, et cetera. So they have a preliminary indication of the cause of the fire. Then what happens, these, after each -- after each intervention call, these statistics, if you will, are then assimilated and produced on to these documents which are then the official records of the fire department with respect to all the interventions during a set period, for example, a year. What we've provided to the Defence on this CD-Rom and then in the hard copies were the entire records of the fire interventions during the period of the indictment and then, of course, because they are broken down by year, the entire year of 1992. But they do have the date so that it's quite clear, looking down the columns of the spreadsheets, exactly what date the various interventions occurred. But again, the Defence has had this information in electronic format for several months now. They have also been provided a hard copy of this, and at this point, Mr. President, the Prosecution does not actually intend on tendering these documents into evidence, but again copies have been provided to the Defence. We've also provided them to Madam Registrar so in the event it becomes relevant or the Trial Chamber itself wants these documents, we have multiple copies available for all the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanation, Mr. Mundis. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, regarding the question of CD-Roms, I personally wrote to the Prosecution to tell them that the system is not reliable and that the Defence cannot rely on it. So regarding that particular problem, this is one matter, the CD-Roms. Another matter, Mr. President, is that this Defence team and especially myself, your servant, worked very long hours in order to examine all these documents which, Mr. President, of the first page carry a characteristic stamp of documents that will be tendered by the Prosecution to this Trial Chamber. We tried to extract from them as much information as possible. We spent a lot of time on these documents and we are told today that it is not important because we have decided not to tender this as evidence. Mr. President, I don't know whether this can be accepted. I don't know whether documents can be given to the Defence, knowing that the Defence will probably work all night, which I did, on these documents and then, in the morning, come and say it doesn't matter; you exhausted yourself in preparation but we will not be tendering them. Personally, as the Defence counsel of General Galic, I cannot tolerate this, but it is not up to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At this very moment, there's no decision to be made on these documents. Perhaps I could make one general remark, that if one party sees that it might not use in evidence a rather voluminous document which is on the list and which has the appearance of a document being tendered in evidence, that if it comes to a -- if the party changes its mind and thinks that it's not necessary, that that party should indicate this to the other party. And perhaps there's another issue: If I look -- of course, I've not -- this Chamber has not seen the document in any detail. But I don't know whether there's any misunderstanding between the parties, and let me just refer to the telephone directory, the example which I gave before which, of course, is not a real example. If the Prosecution would tender the telephone directory just to indicate that someone was listed in this telephone directory, it should either be clear from the statement previously disclosed that this is the way this telephone directory is going to be used or otherwise perhaps the party using the telephone directory might indicate to the other one that it is not intending to establish the truthfulness of all the numbers listed in this telephone directory, and that they are all correct, because this requires a totally different approach of the other party when studying the document. We haven't seen it in detail, but this is what I urge the parties to do, to make it possible for each other to prepare for the examination, the cross-examination, without any waste of time. And especially with these listings, these very long documents, of course, it could easily happen that one of the parties is concentrating on a totally different issue, different from what the other party intends to do with that document, of course apart from the question on whether the cross-examining party would like to search through these documents to see whether there's anything in it which could assist in its own case presentation. Having given this guidance from the Chamber to the parties, Mr. Mundis, would you please call your next witness. And Mr. Usher, could you assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Prosecution calls Mesud Jusufovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I take advantage of the break, of the pause, to say that the Defence feels, having exhausted itself, that it did not have the necessary time to prepare for this witness and we wish to make it quite clear for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We've taken notice of your observation, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, I think you're Mr. Jusufovic. The Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration before giving testimony in this Court. Mr. Usher will now hand out to you the text of this solemn declaration, and may I invite you to make that declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, having been called as a witness for the Prosecution, you'll first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. You'll then later be cross-examined by counsel for the Defence; and when there are any additional questions the Judges would like to put to you, you'll hear from them. Mr. Mundis, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, for the record, can you please state your full name and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I was born in Sarajevo on the 17th of February, 1960. Mesud Jusufovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, did you continue living in the city of Sarajevo from the time of your birth to the present?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I have been living in Sarajevo all my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a graduate engineer of fire protection and protection at work, but I work as a fire brigade man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what is your current position within the fire brigade

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I'm commander of the professional fire brigade in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long have you been a professional firefighter?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I have been a professional firefighter since 1986.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When did the war begin in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it really began, the shooting started, as far as I can remember, it was the 5th of April when we were celebrating liberation day of Vratnik, a part of Sarajevo, and we had just prepared for the event. But then the shelling started.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In what year was that, Mr. Jusufovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And at that time when the war started in Sarajevo, what was your position within the Sarajevo Fire brigade?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I was, when the war began, I was a chief. I was the third man in the fire brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time when the war started, approximately how many men were employed by the Sarajevo Fire Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war and up until the beginning of the war, there were approximately 150 firefighters. But shortly before the beginning of the aggression, 67 firemen of Serbian origin had left Sarajevo and they no longer worked there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Prior to the departure of these 67 firemen, what was the ethnic composition of the Sarajevo Fire Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Half of them were Serbian origin, and half of them were of Muslim origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the time when the war started in 1992, can you tell us how many fire stations or substations existed in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: We had many fire stations, so I'm going to enumerate them: Bascarsija, Centar, Vogosca, Ilijas, Pale, and the airport. So there were six stations before the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In addition to the approximately 150 firefighters, were there also volunteer or reserve firefighters in the fire brigade at that time?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The volunteer organisations became specialised units of the Territorial Defence, so they counted approximately -- the Civil Defence, and they counted approximately -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the number. Could the witness repeat, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you repeat approximately how many volunteer firefighters there were, please.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: There was approximately 150 of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that's in addition to the 150 professional or full-time firefighters?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those 150 volunteers were placed in five different volunteer associations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In order to clarify, can you tell us, these volunteer firefighters, you said they became specialised units. Can you tell us of what organisation they became specialised units?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Civil Defence, because according to the law then, and the law now, in such situations, volunteer societies become units of the Civil Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And once the war began, did the Civil Defence have any military role?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No. The Civil Defence did not exist for those purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, these 150 volunteer firefighters, were they assigned to the fire stations that you mentioned a few moments ago or did they report to volunteer fire stations, again, at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: They were in volunteer societies, and they had the same duties as professional firefighters. That was their duty during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, can you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber the type and numbers of firefighting equipment that the Sarajevo Fire Brigade had, again, at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The fire brigade of Sarajevo, up until the beginning of the war, was one of the stronger fire brigades on the territory of the former Yugoslavia and even further. However, as of the beginning of 1992, our commander, who was at the time Radomir Spaic, gradually started to transfer our equipment to Pale, to begin with, vehicles and radio links, fuel, and all the kitchens, kitchen equipment, so that on the 5th of April, we were completely not ready because we didn't have -- we had 12 vehicles missing, and all the equipment, almost all the equipment that we had up until that time, we had no longer those equipments. So at the beginning of the aggression, we had 14 vehicles, we had almost no fuel. We didn't have any spare parts, and the situation was very difficult, and they have also abandoned us. Half of the firefighters had left us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, I'm terribly sorry to intervene at this point, but I thought that we were talking -- we were trying actually to avoid terms such as "aggression," "aggressors," and that was the only purpose of my intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, could you please guide the witness. And I will explain to you, Mr. Jusufovic, since this Court still has to establish what happened at that time, we usually do not use words like "aggressor," because whether there was aggression and who was an aggressor still has to be established in this Court. So if you could find more neutral terms, that would benefit the task of this Court. Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, when you use the term "aggressor," what force or forces are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I was thinking of the JNA and the others, our Serbs who had left, who had went on to various mountains and started to shell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say "our Serbs," are you referring to Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I'm referring to Serbs from Bosnia. That's what I said. Even our firefighters who had left, they have also shelled us and they have also shelled our fire station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: As a result of this breakup of the Sarajevo Fire Brigade, did it become necessary to reorganise and restructure the fire brigade due to the large number of firefighters who left?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For that reason, all the firefighters were called up from various brigades who had not left Sarajevo, and this is why these volunteer societies were formed, to replace the firefighters that had left. And so this is why we had all spread within the volunteer societies and our departments in order to be able to prepare, accomplish our task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Once the war began, approximately how many firefighters in total, to include the professionals and the reserve, how many firefighters did you have in the Sarajevo Fire Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I would not be able to tell you the exact figure because it changed often. There were a lot of people who died. A lot of people were wounded. But during the war in the professional fire brigade, I would say that it was approximately 120 to 150 firefighters, and that counts also for the volunteer, for the volunteers. So let's say, during the war, we were approximately 300 altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did these firefighters continue to man all of the fire stations in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before Kenan Slinic became commander, he proceeded to reorganise everything, and he called people to start working, and this is when we began work. And those who had not died and who actually were not wounded ended up being firefighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You mentioned shelling a few moments ago. Do you recall approximately when the shelling started?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of April. There was on Vratnik, in the part of Sarajevo, there was a festivity going on. In 1945, on the 5th of April, Vratnik was liberated then, and every year we would celebrate that date. And we had started to prepare for this festivity, and this is when the shelling began.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, I would like to focus your attention now on the period after 10 September, 1992. Did the shelling of the city of Sarajevo continue after 10 September, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The shelling of Sarajevo lasted during the whole war, up until the month of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: April of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Up to Dayton. I'm sorry, the interpreter is correcting itself.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I said that the shelling of Sarajevo started on the 5th of April, 1992, and it lasted up until 1996, up until Dayton, up until the 31st of January, 1996. This is when the special units of the Civil Defence were dismantled, and this is up until the Dayton agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Based on your experience in the city of Sarajevo during the period after 10 September, 1992, was there a particular modus operandi of the shelling as it related to the fire brigade?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Those who were shelling from the surrounding hills, they were targeting Sarajevo. And when they wanted to make sure that something was burning, to set up something on fire, they did not proceed this in a military way. And I believe personally that they wanted to burn Sarajevo completely so that they make sure that we have no place to live any more and that we had to leave. So first they would cut the water supply. They had all the taps within their vicinity, so they would close the taps, and this is when they started to also shell our units in Skenderija. And then they would set some monument on fire, whether a historical monument or a residential building, and then they would protect that installation. In Sarajevo, we used to say, when something is burning, you better leave, you better run away because those who had set that installation on fire from the surrounding hills, they were making sure that we were not able to come and put out the fire. And this is the reason why we were scattered at few different places. So when they were targeting one of our installations, we were able to go to the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you indicate that they were shelling from the surrounding hills, do you know which force or forces controlled the surrounding hills?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian army of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, as part of these attacks, did the fire stations, were they shelled at any time?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all the fire stations were shelled. The firemen, the vehicles, the fire vehicles and the stations, everything was being targeted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will intervene at this point, if I may, with regards to the French transcript. It should be said that in the French transcript, we should be talking about fire stations. This is what we see in the English transcript, but this is the reason why I'm intervening. This was a very important intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what it says in the French transcript, what the confusion is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. In the French transcript, from what I heard from the interpreters that I'm following, they were talking about "casernes" or stations. "Caserne" in French, "caserne" has a military connotation, so this is why I wanted to make sure we're talking about a fire station, so it is a "caserne de sapeurs-pompiers." So those are only stations that are destined, that are fire stations. These are not military stations. The confusion was perhaps existing in the French transcript, but now it's all cleared up. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, you were mentioning shelling attacks on fire stations. Can you describe for us whether the stations were shelled before other parts of the city, at the same time as other parts of the city, or after other parts of the city were shelled on a particular day?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The most important shelling was, for instance, when they would set something on fire, they would not allow us to come out. So when there was a fire going on somewhere, they would shell us at that point so that we cannot go out and put out the fire. That was the reason for the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And during the period after September 10th, 1992, through the middle of 1994, were any firefighters killed by shelling while they were in the fire stations?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: During this period, on the 28th of September, 1992, our station was shelled, the station in Stup. And this is when a fireman was killed. His name was Kalabusic, Sudzia, and he was actually trying to fix a vehicle in the garage. The other firefighters were in the bathroom. That's where they fled. And this is why they stayed alive. He was trying to fix a vehicle, and he died.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now again, during the same period, from September 10th, 1992, through the middle of 1994, were any firefighters wounded by shelling attacks while they were in the fire stations?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: During this period of time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jusufovic, can you briefly describe for the benefit of the Trial Chamber the type of firefighting equipment, and specifically the type of firefighting trucks that the fire brigade had available to it during the same period, that is, 10 September 1992 through the middle of 1994, how many trucks and what type of trucks they were?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: We had 14 fire brigade vehicles. I just wanted to say that today, we have 56 of those vehicles, for instance, to give you an example. Those were older vehicles. And at that time, they were shelled at least twice, so each of these vehicles was hit. And sometimes we would dismantle a vehicle and help create a new one. We were always having problems with the hoses, and they were also hit. So we were not able to put out the fire on higher up, on higher positions, because the hoses would break. We didn't have any fuel. The firefighters had no food.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were these 14 vehicles that you had all of the same type, or were they different types of fire trucks; and if they were different, can you please tell us what type of fire truck they were?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: They were different fire trucks. Some of them were Mercedes, some of them were Magirus TAM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did all of these fire trucks have water-carrying and water-pumping capacity?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Those were vehicles equipped with water tanks and they also had a hose and a pump.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the water capacity of these trucks that the fire brigade had during this period?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The fire vehicles were different. Some could comprise 1 ton of water. Others, 8 tons of water. We had four vehicles that could take up 8 tons of water.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where did the fire brigade obtain its water supply for these trucks during this time period?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The only place where we were able to obtain water was from a factory called the brewery because there was a well situated there, and this is the only place where we were able to get water. But the Serbian army was always closing the water down so that Sarajevo, for the most part, was left without water. And especially when there was a fire going on somewhere, they would make sure that they put the water -- turn the water taps off. And that was the only place where we could get our water supply. And it was very dangerous to get to this brewery because it was always under constant shelling. And our vehicles were also being shelled during the trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: These four vehicles that could carry 8 tons of water, how long would 8 tons of water last while you were putting out a fire?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult to say because it was not always the same. Sometimes we use one hose, sometimes ten hoses. But let's say if it was working at full capacity, it would last five minutes. But we never worked with full capacity hoses, from 10 to 12 hoses. We never did that. But all these vehicles didn't mean anything, because at one point if you have 18 fires to put out, it was very difficult, and those were large fires. These kinds of fires during peace times would happen maybe once every four years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the fire brigade have a means of classifying fires? You talk about "these kinds of fires during peace times." Was there a fire classification system that was employed by the Sarajevo Fire Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was a classification system. When we talk about these large fires, they were classified in a special way. For the period for which we're talking, as of the 11th of September, there was about a hundred of those large fires, because during -- throughout the war, there were 240 of them. But talking about this particular period of time, there was about a hundred of them. I didn't count them, but I think so. So during peacetime, during peace times actually, something like this would happen over a period of 500 years. So each of these large fires represented for us what for you the 11th of September would mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me make sure that I understand what you've said. During the period from 10 September 1992 through the middle of 1994, you're saying there were approximately 100 of these large fires. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that during peacetime, you would expect a large fire such as each of these 100 to only occur approximately once every five years?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what -- how would you characterise one of these large fires? What do you mean by "a large fire"?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That means when we get there, it probably represents a fire occurring with a skyscraper. So that means that a few apartments would be set on fire. Usually when we would arrive, all the citizens would try to escape, and we would try to reach the top floors. This is why I wanted to compare it with the 11th of September. It was very difficult for us to put out such a large fire. It is even difficult when there is no war going on; but during the wartime, it was more difficult because there was no electricity, no water. We had to crawl on the floor. During all the time of our intervention, we were still being shelled. We were being fired on. We had to crawl in order not to perish.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Why did you have to crawl?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Because they were always shooting on us, either with shelling or, if they were closer, with automatic weapons, with rifles. We were -- we would even go to try to put out a fire, and we would be shot at with pistols. They were close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know what type of artillery weapons or other type of larger scale weapons were being used on the city?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were using shells, but there were also phosphorus grenades amongst those. And one of the targets -- one of their purposes what they wanted to achieve is to set an installation on fire. And then they would protect that site so that we cannot approach it. And they were firing on us to try to stop us -- prevent us from actually going there to put out the fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What would happen when a phosphorus grenade would strike a building?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The whole building is set on fire so it is very difficult to extinguish it. These are shells that provoke fires.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do these phosphorus shells have certain types of chemicals in them that would help them burn?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know exactly what chemicals they are, but they are always used in war. They were used in our case to burn our houses, apartments, so that we would have no place to live.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of buildings or structures were targeted during the period of time that we have been discussing?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: During this period of time, and also throughout the war, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. everything was a target in Sarajevo. Whatever the citizens of Sarajevo used was shelled, from historical buildings on, especially places where there were books because the Serbs didn't seem to like books. So they had a special attitude towards these places. Also, apartment blocks, high-rise buildings, because once a high-rise building burns out, then some hundred families have nowhere to live and they have no other choice but to leave Sarajevo. So everything was a target, from hospitals, kindergartens, and especially this Pivara or brewery, where there was water. And wherever they knew there were crowds, there were a lot of people, like bread lines or water lines, a lot of people got killed. So everything that was of any use to the citizens of Sarajevo was shelled so that they would be deprived of it and they would have to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You mentioned water lines. Did there come a time when the fire brigade assisted with dispensing water to the residents of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the fire brigade did assist the citizen in every possible way, including distribution of water, because the only source, as I said, was in this factory called Pivara, the brewery, and the citizens had to cover 10 or 12 kilometres, some even more, to get a jerry can of water or as much as they could carry. It was for that reason that we would distribute water to the citizens, depending on the amount of fuel we had. Usually, when a high-ranking international official was coming to Sarajevo, then the shelling would pause, and that would give us a chance to distribute water to the citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did any of the fire trucks that were distributing water come under shelling or sniping attack while distributing water to the civilians?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this would happen regularly. At Vratnik, for instance, in front of the Fire Brigade station in 1993, when we were distributing water, a shell fell and five or six people were injured. A young woman was killed because she was a voluntary firefighter. Her name was Rubina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know if the Holiday Inn hotel came under artillery fire during the period from 10 September, 1992, through the middle of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The Holiday Inn was a very popular target. They were constantly targeting the Holiday Inn. I think the reason was that there were a lot of reporters in the Holiday Inn, even some ambassadors. And all our hotels were set on fire, and the Holiday Inn was the only one that remained so that the reporters and officials -- if the reporters and officials had gone to Ilidza, they probably thought that their reports would have been different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many times the Holiday Inn was struck during this period?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The Holiday Inn, as it is in an open area, so when there's a fire there, it's very difficult to reach it. We went there I don't know how many times, and then we had to flee and go back. For that reason, we set up a fire brigade team there which throughout this period was there all the time. Firefighters were in the Holiday Inn, and there was a fire brigade engine in the basement. And throughout the hotel, we distributed hoses so that when it caught fire from an incendiary shell, the firefighters would put it out immediately, and they intervened about 500 times. So it means that the hotel was set on fire some 500 times, but there were many more shells, in fact, because not every shell starts a fire. Not every shell is an incendiary shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were there other locations in the city of Sarajevo that were shelled so frequently that you set up small fire stations inside the building?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the Holiday Inn, there was also the Presidency building and the radio-television building. These were also frequent targets, and it was very difficult for us to have access to them, to reach them, so that we had three or four men in the TV. And in the Presidency, there was one firefighter with a fire extinguisher who would act with that extinguisher. And if it was a larger scale fire, then the fire brigade would come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During this period, did the fire brigade have adequate communication equipment to enable you to communicate with each other?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The communications, as I said at the beginning, were all taken to Pale before the war so that we didn't have in our possession much. We had some old communications in the vehicles themselves, installations that were 40 years old. And our repeater station or relay station through which we were able to communicate was on Trebevic, and it was silenced immediately and we couldn't use it any more. Because this hill was under the control of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You mentioned a few moments ago fighting fires in skyscrapers. Approximately how many skyscrapers were there in the city of Sarajevo in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the number. I really can't tell you how many there were. There were many, and many were burnt out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, how do you define a skyscraper?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Sarajevo skyscrapers have about 20 storeys.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you give us an approximation as to the number of buildings in Sarajevo that had 20 or more storeys? Were there five, ten, twenty, fifty, a hundred such buildings? Just a rough estimation of how many skyscrapers in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I think between fifty and a hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And approximately how many of those buildings were set on fire due to shelling during this period?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot guarantee the figure, but I think there isn't one high-rise building that wasn't set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the fire brigade have adequate equipment to fight fires in buildings that were 20 storeys high during this time period?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1992, German firefighters came to Sarajevo and brought with them fire hoses, and from that moment on, we were able to extinguish fires in such buildings as well. We also had fire steps to extinguish fires from the outside. We attempted to use them a couple of times but we were sniped at immediately, so that in this period of time, we didn't dare use those steps because we would have all been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: By steps, do you mean ladders?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, mechanical ladders attached to vehicles. They can reach up to 44 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how many floors would that be, 44 metres?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: About 13 floors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So a fire, say, on the 15th or 18th or 20th floor would be unaccessible with these mechanical ladders. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But we couldn't use the ladders at all because if anyone was to climb on a ladder, he would be dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber how you fought fires under these conditions, that is, during shelling and sniping? How would you respond to a fire, what would you do when you got to the scene of a fire, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was very difficult to reach the scene. So first of all, we had to leave our station, which was under fire, and then in the streets, along the whole route, we would be targeted with shells and snipers. When we finally managed to reach the scene, we didn't dare go in through the door because that is what we did at the beginning. So many of us were killed and wounded. So we had to see from which side we were protected from artillery fire. So we would break through a wall and enter the building, the high-rise building. Everyone would flee from the high-rise as well as from the surrounding buildings. And as I said, it was most dangerous to be close to a fire because we knew that the shelling would start then. Because while they were extinguishing the fire, 200 or 300 shells would fall on that building. So the vehicle which was outside the building, and if the fire was on the 20th floor, we had to tie up the hoses and climb up to the 20th floor. This was very difficult, especially at nighttime and when there was no electricity, and this was often. And also, you had to be careful as you moved. Wherever there was a window, a bullet could come in. So whenever you reached a window, you had to crawl by it. And once we reached the fire and started extinguishing it, then these people on the hills would set fire to the floors below, maybe the 10th floor or the 5th floor. And the fire would burst into flames, and then we firefighters would be exposed to choking so that we had to run for our lives. Very often the firefighters themselves had to flee to safety. For some reason, we were shelled most. And the citizens were aware of this, and they fled from us during the war because wherever we were, there was shelling. And they wouldn't let us put the fire out because, for them, it was a success when a high-rise building burned out because a hundred families had nowhere to live and that would mean a hundred families less in Sarajevo, and they would be closer to their aim. And that is why they didn't like us, because we wouldn't let them set our town on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would ask that the witness now be shown a video which is marked P3609.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [No microphone]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, we are going to show you a video at the moment and I would like you to watch that video. Then, at the completion of that video, I will ask you a few questions about what you see on the screen in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, having seen that video, did you recognise the building that was in that videotape?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where is that building?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It's across the road from the electricity distribution building, and I was in charge of the extinguishing of the distribution building. And I saw this building being set on fire, and I called up for new forces to come to this building which was called "sibica" or "match box," and then I switched to that building as well because they needed more firefighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So you actually participated in extinguishing the fire in the building that we just saw on the videotape?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for us what exactly you saw in the videotape.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember now which floor it was, but it was quite high up. It was higher than 15. And the firefighters -- so I actually saw it starting to burn. The firefighters came and started extinguishing it, and then they set fire with incendiary shells, as you could see on this video. They were shooting, and you could see a water seeping out. The firefighter was lying down and that is why he didn't get killed. So they set fire to a lower floor so that we had to save the citizens below as well as the firefighters. We tried to use this vehicle for rescuing from high up; however, we were immediately shot at, even though this side had some protection. So we couldn't use this method. And then the firefighters as well as the citizens started running down the rails, the hand rails of the steps, which was very dangerous, of course. But these were citizens of Sarajevo. They probably were not meant to live.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The videotape clearly showed people climbing down balconies on the outside wall of the building. Was that a practice that you saw on more than one occasion in putting out fires in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: What you saw, a well-trained firefighter, an athlete, could do this but that is what the citizens of Sarajevo had to be in order to survive everything that these from the hills served upon us. So this happened quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You mentioned a few moments ago that as you were putting out fires, "they didn't like you." Can you tell us who you meant by "they"?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I meant this army of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What was the relationship like between the people of Sarajevo and the fire brigade during the war?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The citizens liked the firefighters, because the firefighters were the only people who could help them and who did help them in situations like these. So what worse can happen to a man than when his apartment or house is burnt down? And the firefighters would come and put out the fire and save what could be saved. When a house is destroyed by shelling, we would pull out the men and the children from the rubble. One such case was when an intervention occurred prior to this period, 11 people were wounded. About 1.000 people came to the hospital to give their blood for their firefighters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, during the period from 10 September 1992 to the middle of 1994, where did you and your family live?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I lived first at Vratnik in my mother's house. And that is where a shell fell through the ceiling and hit the floor, but it didn't explode, so that both I, my wife, and children survived. After that, I moved to an apartment, again, in Vratnik, and there also a shell came through the ceiling and left holes in the mattresses we slept on. However, 5 minutes prior to that, I had taken my wife and children to the basement. After that, I lived in my sister's apartment in Alipasin Most. Here again, several bullets came in. I was mostly with the fire brigade because the state of emergency was continuous. It was difficult to reach work. People got killed as they went to work or went home after work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time when your family moved into the fire brigade building with you?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: My family did not, but many families did come to the fire brigade. Those firefighters whose house was destroyed or burnt had nowhere to live, would come to the fire brigade station. I had somewhere to live. There were some 15 families living in our offices, but mostly in the basement because we have a basement in the fire brigade station. And there were some 15 families living there. And as the commander, this was an advantage because the firefighters were there. They didn't have to come and go to work because some would get killed on the way home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how long did these 15 families reside in the basement of the fire brigade station?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe for the Trial Chamber the effect of the shelling and sniping campaign on your own family?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It had an adverse effect. My wife and two children did not leave the basement for 18 months. There was no window, no daylight. And there's never any electricity. It was very hard. I had a large number of casualties. My brother-in-law was killed. My nephew of 11 lost his leg. I had to protect him in hospital because he didn't believe that there were no Chetniks in the hospital, and he was an 11-year-old child. The traumas have affected all of us, including the firefighters. It was a traumatic experience. The first time that ten of us firefighters went to Austria, in Split, we walked around -- and this was in 1998. We were walking along the seaside and a ship anchored, and we heard a whistle. And we all threw ourselves to the ground. People thought that we had gone mad. We thought it was a shell. So you see, the memory stuck in our minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. I have approximately 10 to 15 more minutes with this witness, and I'm about to go into an area that I think would go past the 10.30 normal period where we take a recess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then I prefer to have a break. We'll adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, you may proceed to examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, I'd like to focus your attention now again on the period from 10 September 1992 through the middle of 1994. Can you describe what relationship there was between the fire brigade and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: There was no relationship at all. The fire brigade was a civilian association. We had nothing to do with the army, and we had nothing to do with the police either. We were part of the civilian defence, and we were there to save the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the fire brigade have any kind of radios or other communication devices that would allow them to communicate with the army of BH?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The fire brigade had a radio station, but it was on the fire frequency, fire brigade frequencies. Every state has a special frequency for the fire brigade and those frequencies were quite different from any other frequencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During the period of the war in Sarajevo, did you personally serve in the ABiH at any time?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was never within the army of the ABiH, but during the first month, so when the shelling began on the 5th of April, and for a whole month, the neighbours and myself, we had organised ourselves in that portion of Vratnik because we saw on television what was going on in Croatia. They were killing people, and we also heard from our ancestors what the Chetniks did in the Second World War. So during that one-month period, myself and my neighbours, we made some makeshift weapons from various tubes, and we wanted to protect our families.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But your involvement with this voluntary defence of your neighbourhood was over by the summer of 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. At the end of the month of May, I went back to the fire brigade because that was my job, to work there. I was also a volunteer fireman, and that's the only thing that I know how to do and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that's the thing I do best.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did other members of the fire brigade -- or did any members of the fire brigade serve at the same time in the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No, because that was impossible. There wasn't enough of us. For the most part, we were always working. Sometimes during the period of after working seven days, we were able to go home. After working for 12 hours, for instance. Because there were fire everywhere, and when we would go to put out a fire, it would happen that for two to three days we would not come back home. Because, for instance, after a shelling incident, we had to protect -- we had to protect and we wanted to put out the fire. But what would happen is that the neighbouring facilities would also start burning, so we had to put out the fire for two to three days sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, Mr. Jusufovic, that members of the fire brigade were exempt from serving in the army of the BH?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, all the men had to be somewhere. But I do agree with the fact that we were exempt because people who were in the fire brigade, other people who were within the civilian defence, everybody who had a working duty. Because during the war, some people also went to work. They had to go sometimes for 10 kilometres under a rain of shells to go to work. So somebody had -- everybody had to do something, so it was either a working obligation; if you had a working obligation, you didn't have to be a member of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, Mr. Jusufovic, that during the war, you were in several hundred buildings in Sarajevo extinguishing fires?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In how many of those buildings did you encounter ABiH command posts or headquarter facilities?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Never. They were all civilian buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In any of those buildings did you see any kind of military infrastructure or offices or rooms that were used by the military or barracks that were used by the military?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No. The only military infrastructure that we intervened for was the Marsal Tita barracks, and when they shelled those barracks, this is when we had to intervene and try to put out the fire, and we were helped by the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: During any of the fires that you helped to extinguish, did you encounter any military weapons, any rifles, machine-guns, or any type of munitions in any of those buildings?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No. Not at all, except when we had to put out the fire during the shelling of the UNPROFOR barracks and the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In entering any of the civilian buildings, did anyone ever warn you that there were explosives or any kind of military hardware or equipment that might pose a danger for the members of the fire brigade?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No, it never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In which areas of the city of Sarajevo did the fire brigade operate?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The fire brigade operated in the city centre of Sarajevo, aside from those areas that were occupied. I'm talking about Grbavica, Ilidza, Ilijas, Vogosca. It was always part of Sarajevo. Those parts were still part of Sarajevo but at the time we could not intervene on those areas because those areas were occupied. And during one portion of the war, we were also not able to go to Dobrinja because we couldn't get through. And this is why -- there was a volunteer association there, and they would be in charge to put out the fires in that area. We could also not go to Hrasnica because it was impossible for us to get through, but it was also a volunteer association there, and they were in charge to put out the fires.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You mentioned areas that were occupied, to use your term. What force or forces were occupying those areas?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Those were forces; at the very beginning of the war, it was the JNA forces, together with the Bosnian Serbs. And then they changed signs. Instead of the five-star -- instead of the star, they would change the sign, and the link that existed between the JNA and the military, the Serbian military men, we could see when on Grbavica, there was a fire set to the building of Union Invest, and this is today where we have the building of the high representative. When our firemen were captured at the airport, together with their vehicles, the SDS from Grbavica, the headquarters, called us to go and to put out the fire there. That was at the beginning of the war. And when we said that our vehicles were at the airport, they ordered a JNA colonel to actually let us through, and they did. It was not linked, this period of time, but this was the link that existed, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Is it fair then, Mr. Jusufovic, to say that the fire brigade was limited to those areas that were controlled by the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jusufovic. The Prosecution has no further questions at this time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, is it you who is going to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honour, we, however, expect that the Chamber would allow us -- that my colleague does ask a few questions, if it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll allow that. As you know, not simultaneously but one after another. And if you'd please stay within the time used by the examination-in-chief. I'm just saying, because yesterday, a bit more time was taken. I didn't interfere, but therefore sometimes I ask at the beginning to keep it mind. Sometimes I do it halfway, sometimes at the end. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Jusufovic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you be able to confirm to us that on the 21st of June, 1999, and the 24th of June, 1999, you made a statement to the Prosecution's office?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I probably did.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you sign and did you confirm in that way that the statement that was given was the truth and everything you said was put down in writing?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I signed, and it's everything I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to show you a document. It is a conversation that you had with the investigators of the Prosecution's office on the year 2000 and 2001, in October and in September. Do you remember this? Do you remember that you had an interview?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that there were some interviews, but I could not tell you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since the witness confirmed this, I consider that it is not necessary to submit him this statement. Maybe he could just confirm to us that his statement -- that his signature is on the statement, but that is the reason why I didn't show the statement to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think usually there's no -- until now, we always have had confirmations of the signatures. So if there's no specific reason, I think -- and if the witness has testified that he signed a statement and he has declared, according to the truth, it might be not necessary always to show the signature. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution would concur with that. However, Mr. President, it might be just an error in the translation or the record, Ms. Pilipovic also refers to documents concerning interviews in 2000, 2001. On those occasions, signed statements were not taken from the witness. Simply, information reports were prepared which were then disclosed to the Defence. The witness indeed signed a witness statement in 1999, however, the documents in the year 2001 were not signed witness statements. And those, to my knowledge, Mr. President, have never been shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, this is the first time you told me about the signature. It seems to be different from other moments. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I wish to reply. I did not say that this was a statement. I just merely wanted to confirm whether the witness had an interview, and I know what can be written on an information report that is given to the Defence. I am fully aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you told us that you lived in Alipasino Polje?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I said that for a certain period of time, I lived in Alipasino Polje, but that was for about one month.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: During the relevant period, that is to say, after the 10th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say after the 10th of September, of what year are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you be more precise and tell us during which period of time and when did you live in Sarajevo for the longer period?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: In Vratnik. I had an apartment in Vratnik, and this is where I lived for the longer period of time, and in Alipasino Polje, when my brother-in-law died and when my niece -- when my nephew remained without the leg, they were evacuated to the United States. So the apartment was empty and this is where we lived for about one month, because we had about 15 bullets that entered my apartment and it was dangerous for the children.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you were living in Vratnik, you told us that you were drafted and you actually participated to the defence of your neighbourhood. Could you tell us, could you confirm to us that it was from the month of April up until the 15th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you the exact date when I went back to the fire brigade because I first went to the fire association in Vratnik, but that was at the beginning of June or perhaps at the end of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Then when you organised yourself in this manner, were you a local commander? Did you assume that role?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us that after you left your post as a local commander, did the army come to that part of Vratnik?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Those were citizens at the time. When I was there, those were citizens, and we had made some trenches around Vratnik because it was the first area near Pale. We had about 20 hunting rifles and some makeshift rifles made from some tubes, and when I left, it became bigger.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell me and the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just interfere. I feel that the speed is going up. Mr. Jusufovic, you are talking the same language as Ms. Pilipovic does. That means that you can quickly answer, but the translators, the interpreters, need some time to translate. If you would look at your screen, and perhaps give an answer when you see that the text is not moving any more. You see, as long as the translation is going on, the text is moving. When it stops, then perhaps you give the answer. May I remind you as well, Ms. Pilipovic. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, you just told us that you and the citizens of Vratnik had dug up trenches, and you said that you had organised yourselves so that you can defend yourself, and you said that Pale was not far from there. Can you tell us what is the distance between Vratnik and Pale?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: About 5 to 6 kilometres, but I couldn't tell you with precision.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "us," "we," during your testimony, you always talk in the plural. You say "we." Could you tell us who is it that you think of when you say "we"?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I think of myself, of Mesud Jusufovic, Ibro, Himzo, Ejub. I'm talking about us, neighbours, citizens of Vratnik, inhabitants of Vratnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly when you said that your neighbours that you just mentioned, are those Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Names do not mean a thing. I just wanted to tell you that those were neighbours of mine. Those were inhabitants of Vratnik. They were not all Muslim. There were some who were actually Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your part of town where you lived, you say that not everybody was Muslim. Some of them were Goran. Were there also Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The inhabitants of Vratnik comprise 99 per cent of Muslims, but there were also some Serbs, and there was one Goran and one Dragan in one of our units.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Today, you talked to us about headquarters and stations, your fire stations. You told us that they had headquarters. Can you tell us how many municipalities exist in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me for the period before the war, after the war, or during the war?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war and during the war.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Before the war, Sarajevo had ten municipalities. And during the war, the old city, Stari Grad, Centar, and Novo Sarajevo, Novi Grad as well, Ilidza were part of it. Today, Sarajevo comprises all of those with the exception of Pale.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you enumerated the municipalities in Sarajevo, you talked to us about Stari Grad, Novo Sarajevo, Novi Grad, Centar. Are those municipalities that had, for the most part, Muslim inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: You didn't mention the municipality of Ilidza. I never counted them. I didn't know what was the composition of Serbs, of Muslims. I didn't even know how to distinguish them by name.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: But can you confirm to us whether the municipalities of Pale, for instance, or the municipality of Pale, is it part of the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, Grbavica, Lapisnica? Is that part of Dobrinja? Is it part of Ilidza, Trnovo, Ilijas, Vogosca? Were those municipalities in which during the war mainly Serbian population lived and were those municipalities under the control of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Those municipalities and parts of municipalities who were under the Serb control.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the municipalities of Stari Grad, Centar, one part of the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, one part of the municipality of Ilidza, and I believe that part of town is called Hrasnica, that those municipalities were under the control of the ABiH army?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry. I didn't understand your question very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat my question. The municipality of Centar, Novo Sarajevo, one portion of the municipality of Novo Sarajevo, the municipality of Stari Grad, Centar, and part of the municipality of Ilidza, was that part of the municipality under the control of the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you be able to confirm to us whether during the conflict, and we're talking about the period from the month of April 1992, or actually September 1992 up until the month of August 1994, could you confirm to us if in those municipalities front lines were established and that there were conflicts on a daily basis between the two armies?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The front line was there. With regards to the conflicts, we didn't have so much ammunition in order to have fightings every day.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us regarding the ABiH what equipment it had regarding clothing and weapons?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: While I was at Vratnik, we had rifles made out of water pipes, and hunting rifles. Later, the army had some automatic rifles, perhaps -- I don't know how it developed during the war. But I do know that when we were shelled from Lapisnica, this is a distance of some 800 metres. They were sunning and shooting at us, and we had nothing to respond with.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, during your examination-in-chief, you kept saying, "and they shelled us from the hills." Would you agree with me in saying that the hills and mountains surrounding the city of Sarajevo, and I will first mention Igman, Zuc, Hum, Mojmilo, Brijesce, Sokolje, the hill of Grdonja, Colina Kapa, the big and small one below Trebevic, Hrasno, that these were locations, hills and Mount Igman, that throughout the conflict from April 1992 until September 1994 were under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that with precision, but some of the places that you listed I know were under the control of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that Brijesce and Stup were under the control of the 102nd Motorised Brigade, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid that motorised brigade doesn't mean anything to me. Probably -- maybe all of that may be correct but I don't know all these things because I wasn't familiar with them. I didn't have time. We were extinguishing fires.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, you said that in your opinion, the real war in Sarajevo actually started, as you put it, on the day of the liberation of Sarajevo. When you said it really started, did you mean that there was a conflict in Sarajevo before the 5th or 6th of April, the liberation day of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It was on that day that the shells started falling. And before that, there were barricades. The Serbs put up barricades. I don't know whether that was February or March. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that the first barricades in Sarajevo were erected after the Serbian wedding in Bascarsija?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that members, Muslims -- that Muslims also erected barricades?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that in that period, the 1st of March, both Muslim and Serb barricades were erected, as confirmed by many witnesses, and that mixed patrols were formed after that, would you agree with me then, mixed patrols consisting of Serbs, Croats, and Muslims who, in that period, that is in March, controlled and protected the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I am not aware of any Muslim barricades. As far as I can remember, there were mixed patrols between the army and the police.
