utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are confirming that the police was part of these mixed brigades that controlled law and order in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not confirming that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain what was the role, then, of these mixed patrols, as you see them, police formations, of these police formations?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I never saw those mixed units, but I heard on television that there were some discussions with Kukanjac that such mixed units would be formed. I know that very soon after that, the JNA revealed its real aim and none of it took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that the army soon revealed its true face, can you tell us which ethnic groups in those days were members of the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Until then, I mean during the former Yugoslavia, all ethnic groups were represented. I, too, was a soldier of the Yugoslav People's Army but in 1980. But in those days, there were very few Muslims because our recruits did not join the army. They were arrested because they wouldn't go to the army. Many were killed in their sleep.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you tell us that Muslim recruits would not go to the army, can you confirm that already in 1990, in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, a patriotic league had been formed which was, in fact, an army of the SDA which later grew into the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: If there had been such an army, I would not have been defending with a rifle made of water pipes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you're telling us that you were defending the part of town in which you lived with a rifle made of water pipes, that this was in April and May 1992. Can you confirm that in that period of time, in the city of Sarajevo, there were paramilitary formations which controlled the city? One of them was under the leadership of Caco, who is from Vratnik, and you know he has his brigade there and that he was buried there; then there was Juka Prazina's brigade; then Cela's brigade; that these were paramilitary formations which, in the period of March, April, and May, ran the city of Sarajevo and engaged in battle and attacked members of the Yugoslav People's Army. Can you agree with me that that is true?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that. First of all, Caco is not from Vratnik, and he was never in Vratnik, or his unit was never there. And until the 5th of April, there was no army. Who would they attack? From the 6th of April, there were such groups of neighbours and citizens who were protecting their part of town, their wives and children.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If you tell us that as a citizen, you were protecting your parts of town and your homes, can I take it that in the part of town inhabited by Serbs, they, too, had the right to organise themselves and protect their homes?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that because we started the defence after the first shells, so I don't know who shelled Pale, and was Pale ever shelled.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: You told us today that your brigade numbered 150 employed and that there was a division along ethnic lines, as far as I was able to understand, in your brigade. Could you tell us when this division along ethnic lines occurred?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: When the first barricades were organised. There were fire brigades used for that purpose, to erect barricades. It was then that we non-Serbs saw that things were not going in the best direction, and we saw where things were heading. And then the Serbs had a meeting - that's what they said - with Karadzic, and they abandoned the brigade, most of them, 67 of them, to be precise, before the 5th of April. Ten of them stayed on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any Croats within your fire brigade?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: There were Croats as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did they leave the fire brigade?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Most of them stayed behind, but there weren't many Croats, to be quite frank. All of them stayed. Later on, one of them left.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you were telling us today about voluntary societies which became specialised units of the Civil Defence, could you tell us when those voluntary societies were formed? Could you explain? Did they function before the war as well or were they formed after the division that occurred within your fire brigade?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't call it a fire brigade society, a fire brigade. Voluntary societies existed. For example, the Vratnik Fire Brigade Society exists since 1934. The fire brigade society in Novo Sarajevo also was founded that same year. Bjelave, too, I don't know when. Alipasin Most, Ilidza, was operating in Hrasnica. So all these societies had been in existence some 50 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you, as a fire brigade, during the conflict in Sarajevo were operating also in the settlement of Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: We couldn't operate there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the period of 1992, the month of June, that this neighbourhood was set on fire and that it was burning and a special machine known as Voma had been used?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that, nor do I know what that machine is.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: It's a tank called Voma, filled with explosives, and in June 1992, Nedzarici was set on fire. So I'm asking you whether you, with your fire brigade, extinguished the fire in that neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: If there was a fire and if it was in June, we couldn't reach there because whenever we passed by Nedzarici, we were shot at.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you intervened, could you tell us whether you kept any records; and if so, during the day or during a week, how would you make a record of those interventions?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That is our standard procedure. Every leader, the person in charge of an intervention, once it is completed, needs to fill in a special intervention form. And in most cases, we filled them in when we had the paper and when the firefighters returned to the station. But all the interventions were not recorded because, for Dobrinja and Hrasnica, we have no records as we couldn't get there. And also, when you intervene in one place, then from that place, you go to another 15. So we would have a record of only that first intervention.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you are telling us that your records were not quite precise regarding all the interventions that you had during that period? I'm talking about the period of 1992, 1993, and 1994.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Whenever records we kept were in order. There were interventions that were left out because, for the reasons I have given, they could not be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you personally, as the brigade commander, compile reports, annual reports, shall we say, about interventions in certain parts of the city and in certain buildings which, in your opinion, were most affected or were more important buildings? Did you keep such records?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Every year, we have a report on our work, and every year we would hand in that report to the municipal assembly. That was our obligation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you kept records of your interventions, when filling in these statistical forms about those interventions, did you take note of the time and place? Or rather, could you tell us what is the information you entered into those forms? What is it you considered important?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you mean I, personally, or we, the firefighters.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to your services. You are the brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: So this is filled in by the person in charge of that particular intervention, and on this intervention form you enter the date, the hour, the minute, who called up to ask for help, from which number, how long it took to reach the scene, how long it took to localise the fire, to extinguish it, and all those who participated in the operation are listed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In this form, did you also enter the cause of the fire?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did. I omitted to mention that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, what was the most frequent cause of fires in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, the most frequent cause of fires was shelling, intentional setting on fire. And there were other causes, too, which occur in peacetime as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So you're telling us that the intentional targeting was targeting with shells?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with shells and bullets.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us how many interventions you had with fires caused through negligence, unknown reasons, and for technical reasons?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I think that you can find all that in the document I signed. I can't tell you by heart.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, in answer to a question by my learned friend, you said that the command positions and headquarters of the BH army were not familiar to you, that you did not know where they were.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I don't quite understand what you mean. I had nothing to do with the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: My understanding was, and correct me if I am wrong, that when you were asked when you intervened, did you know whether it was a military target or not and whether there was any soldiers or ammunition there, you said that you didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe you misunderstood. My answer was that we never extinguished fires in barracks or headquarters. There weren't any such cases. There may have been some on the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, on the basis of your recollection, can you tell us whether you extinguished fires in schools?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you, perhaps, remember extinguishing a fire in the elementary school Pavle Goranin?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that in Sarajevo, there is an elementary called Pavle Goranin?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I've heard of the name of that school, but I don't know where it is situated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that from the statistical forms that you have provided the Prosecution with and the Prosecution disclosed it to the Defence, there is a frequent mention of a building that you intervened in to extinguish a fire was the elementary school Pavle Goranin. So will you confirm that it was in your report as your interventions?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Whatever is in the report, I agree with, although I personally may not have been involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence would like to read a line from a document that we received from my learned friends, and I have given a copy to my learned friends and also to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence would just like to read from this document. It is a document of the 102nd Motorised Brigade. The commander is Esad Paldum. The document is 0205-6502. It's on the 23rd of May, 1993. It is in the form of an order, and under 1, it says: "Carry out an examination and control of all warehouses and other premises in the barracks at the elementary school Pavle Goranin."

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, when you intervened in the fire that broke out in the Pavle Goranin elementary school, did you know there was a barracks there stationing the soldiers of the 102nd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that particular intervention. You're telling us that it exists, so we probably did intervene. But it should be known that schools were mostly not functioning in this period of time. Who would send their child to school when he would get killed 15 times before getting there? So teachers would go to basements and teach children.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: By saying that schools were not working, are you confirming that the ABiH was using schools as places to station troops?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not confirming that. For instance, the Vratnik elementary school was a popular canteen where humanitarian aid was distributed and food provided for people who had nothing to eat. There was no army there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, I will tell you that one of the witnesses heard, and who lived at Vratnik, said that the elementary school at Vratnik was used as a canteen for the army.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Later on, I don't know. But while I was at Vratnik, Mrkva Ejub ran the canteen for citizens who had nothing to eat.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From your reports in which you listed the interventions by your brigades, it can be seen that you frequently intervened in the factory Vaso Miskin Crni?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, if I tell you that on the 13th of March, 2002, a witness was heard in this Court who, on page 5304, line 19, said that the headquarters of the Territorial Defence and later the headquarters of the 2nd Motorised Brigade was accommodated in the building Vaso Miskin Crni, would you agree with me that in that factory the army was stationed?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that this witness on the 13th of March, 2002, said that the positions of the 2nd Motorised Brigade were in the area of the promenade?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: You're asking me things about the army. I'm a firefighter, and wherever there's a fire, we extinguish it. We now even go to Lukavica, even to Turkey. We don't care what is burning. Wherever there's a fire, we go to extinguish it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, in your examination-in-chief, you told us about buildings and the shelling of buildings inhabited by civilians. If I tell you that the Loris building is an apartment building and that there is a commercial enterprise in the ground floor where troops were stationed, would you agree with me that troops were also stationed in apartment buildings inhabited by the citizens of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Probably not in apartment buildings. As for Loris, there may have probably been soldiers because that was at the very front line. If there hadn't been any soldiers there, then it probably wouldn't be ours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If you say that in the Loris building, which was also an apartment building, and the business premises were used for the needs of the army, and that that was the front line, would you agree with me then that on that front line there were battles being fought between the two armies?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I know that when we came to extinguish fires at the Loris building, people were living there. And Loris has ten entrances, and maybe in one of those entrances or in some of those flats, there may have been soldiers. But people were living there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that during the armed operations, and I'm talking specifically about the front line at the Pere Kosoric Square where the Loris building is situated, a fire could have occurred due to the impact of weapons? Could a fire have occurred accidentally?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Fires were always started by weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: From the records that you have provided my learned friends with, it can be seen that you very frequently intervened in the area of the Bristol Hotel where there were fires. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know which area you mean. Bristol was burnt down -- burnt out.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that a witness who testified in this courtroom said that the positions and the troops of the 2nd Motorised Brigade were stationed in the Bristol Hotel, in the economic school, and the electrical engineering faculty, and that that was the front line along the Miljacka River, and that in this part of the city battles were very frequent, would you agree with me that, due to armed operations by the ABiH and the VRS, fires did break out and that that was the reason for the fire in the Bristol Hotel, in the school, and the reason for your interventions there?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that. I don't know about Bristol. Bristol was burnt earlier on. I don't remember any particular interventions around there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: During your interventions, during the year of 1992, 1993 and 1994, did you ever intervene for the kindergarten on Cengic Vila and the kindergarten in Otes?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: If there was a report of this event, then we did intervene. I do not remember it personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: If I tell you from the Document 0205-6493, it's a document that comes from the 102nd Motorised Brigade, and if I show you this document, the document is destined to the 1st Corps command, and the following, it says: "Due to the changing of zone of responsibility of the 102nd Motorised Brigade, there is a necessity for distribution of electricity on our localities. We're talking about the factory Gisa, the long-distance power lines, Magros, Valter Peric, Klinerja [phoen] and the elementary school Slobodan Vukovic, the Metabin [phoen] gas works, then the primary school Petar Dokic, and the nursery school, the basis of Stela, the nursery school of Otoka, the Marsal Tita barracks, the Energoinvest building, the kindergarten 8th March on Cengic Vila, the school called Pavle Goranin, and Hotel Zagreb." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. From your evidentiary leaflets, records that you actually showed showed the Prosecution and that the Prosecution showed us, all these installations are listed. And the 102nd Motorised Brigade is listed in there, and those were the reasons for the fires, and you recorded that very often you had to intervene on those buildings that I just enumerated to you. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: We intervened wherever there was a fire and whenever we were able to get to the fire. And every time we would try to do our job, we were always shelled on and shot at.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me to say that the reason for these fires, and especially the reason for the fires on the buildings that I just mentioned to you, were always linked to the armed operations and the battles that took place in Sarajevo between two armies?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree with you, and I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you do not know, does it mean that you also don't know who is responsible for the shelling and what the reason for the fires on those buildings are?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I do know who was the author of the shelling, but when the shell falls on a building, I don't know what is that person's real reason aside from, of course, killing.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, during the time when you were a commander of the brigade or, rather, before you became the brigade commander, did you work somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I started working at the brigade in 1986. On the 11th of September, 1992, I became the commander -- deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that up until 1986, you worked in the factory called Pretis Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: In the factory Pretis Vogosca, I worked in 1980 for the period of three months and 20 days. After this period of time I worked as a taxi driver, and then I started my employment within the fire brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you become the commander of the brigade after the death of your colleague Kenan Slinic?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I was his deputy, and when he died, I became the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: While you were carrying out your duties as the commander of the brigade and while you were also working as a deputy commander of the same brigade in 1992, 1993, and 1994, did you have any meetings or a meetings with Mr. Stjepan Siber? Did you get together?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: With Stjepan Siber, I never got together with him. I never had a meeting with him.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if your collaborators ever went to have a meeting with Mr. Stjepan Siber?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No fireman had the necessity to go to have a meeting with Stjepan Siber, but I know that Kenan Slinic was in good terms with everybody, and we knew that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Mr. Stjepan Siber published his diary about the events in Sarajevo in 1992, 1993, and 1994?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do know that he published something.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in that diary that he wrote, he also mentions the fire brigade and he talks about some people from your fire brigade?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I had heard about something. I think that he mentions Kenan Slinic. There was something with him. But I did not read that diary.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence, with your permission, would like to show the witness an excerpt from the book win by Mr. Stjepan Siber. It's four lines. I have given to my learned friends a copy of this document, as well as to the interpreters. We're talking about the 178th page of the book written by Mr. Stjepan Siber. We are talking about the 19th of August, 1993. Number 3, item 3. "Around noon, the firefighters from Sarajevo came to visit me and -- "

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, could you please --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, you'd like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For the record, Mr. President, Ms. Pilipovic did, in fact, provide a copy of this to us during the last break. Unfortunately, there's no English version of this available so I'm not aware of exactly what the document says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I know that the book has played a role before. Is this true, Ms. Pilipovic, that you provided the --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I see at least that Mr. Mundis is not taking his headphones off. What's your position? I didn't hear any firm objection against reading four lines out of the book. Am I right in my understanding? Although I do understand that you don't like to be confronted with a --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Exactly, and perhaps we'll raise an objection once we've heard the interpreter render the English version. But simply to indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Pilipovic, if you'd please first read the four lines, and if there would then be an objection by the Prosecution, would you please wait to put the question to the witness in relation to the four lines. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. "Around noon, I was visited by firefighters from Sarajevo. They were complaining to me about the commander of the brigade, Mesud Jusufovic, who had taken on the fire brigade after the death of Kenan Slinic. They say that he is proceeding to ethnic division and purges, and he is underestimating the Croats and the Serbs. Firefighters were complaining to this because -- while they were sitting in my office and what is interesting is that they were all Muslims. They say that Jusufovic is pretending to be very much of a religious man, and they say that they have proof that he drinks a lot, gets drink, and he mistreats the other firefighters."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask a question in this respect. "Around noon," that may be 365 days a year. Could you indicate what time period this part of the book deals with so that we have an impression on...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was the month of August 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: So on the 19th of August, 1993, around noon. I have but one question, Mr. Jusufovic. You did hear what Mr. Siber wrote. In view of your -- the answers given by you during the examination-in-chief and the fact that you very often used the word "us" and "them," is it true that you were proceeding to an ethnic division and that you were mistreating people?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I did not know that this was written. It was only two months after I became commander. I never heard a bigger stupidity in my life because in the fire brigade, in our fire brigade, there wasn't one Serb or one Croat that didn't have an important position. And since I became commander, not one of them left the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that there is no Serb or Croat occupying an important post, for what period of time are you actually talking?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the period of time from the moment I became commander. There was one Croat who was creating problems. He would get drunk, and Kenan Slinic replaced him, not myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Are you telling us that today there are Serbs and Croats that occupy important position within your fire brigade?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that is what I am saying. They have always been there. They have always done this, and they will always be there in this capacity.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interfere. I see that there's some problem. The witness, at least in the English text, testified, "there wasn't one Serb or one Croat that did not have an important position." Your next question, at least in the English version, Ms. Pilipovic, was: "When you say that there was no Serb or Croat occupying an important post." That seems to be the opposite. I don't know whether it's a translation problem, but at least in the English version it might demonstrate confusion. But if you say you're not confused, I'm only happy.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my question was not interpreted correctly. And with your leave, I will repeat -- reiterate my question to the witness. I believe that the witness did understand, however.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you say that during all the period in question while you were the commander of the brigade, within the fire brigade, Serbs and Croats occupied important positions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who is your deputy today within the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Presently, we do not have a deputy because according to the new system, job description, that post does not exist.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Who was there before?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It was Cesko Huso.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: There is a fire brigade unit almost in every municipality today?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many fire brigade units are there?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Eight.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Out of these eight fire brigade units, can you tell us how many commanders are of Serbian ethnicity, how many Croat, how many Muslim? I'm talking about units.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The commander, the deputy, and all the chiefs of the brigade, and there's also a ninth centre, the dispatching centre, so for those units there's one Croat, one Serb, and all the other ones are Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this puts an end to my portion of this cross-examination. I will consult my colleague to see if he has some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have perhaps one additional question to you, Ms. Pilipovic. You confronted the witness with a question about -- you started with, "If I tell you that a witness who testified in this courtroom said that the positions and the troops of the 2nd Motorised Brigade were stationed in the Bristol Hotel, in the economic school, and the electrical engineering faculty, and that it was the front line along the river," could you please give me the source where this testimony was given in this Court because I have something different in my recollection?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have written down, page 5313, lines from 4 to 10. And it's from the transcript on the 13th of March. I could tell you the name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Sabljica.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what transcript you are using, the English transcript or...? And perhaps you'd please repeat the lines. 5313, because -- let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lines 4, 10, and 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what version you're using, but that's not at least in my transcript on page 5313. What I found, as a matter of fact, is on page 5308, and if it would assist you, I'd just tell you what the testimony of the witness was. Mr. Sabljica testified that: "The positions were in front of the building of the economic school, in the vicinity of the Bristol Hotel, somewhere in front of the engineering school, and the headquarters was at the same location where the Territorial Defence headquarters used to be, that is, within the compound of Vaso Miskin Crni factory." You did put to the witness that there was testimony that the troops were in the Bristol Hotel, which is not, at least, what the witness testified on the page I found. What you did later on, you asked him to mark the Bristol Hotel. You didn't ask him to mark where the troops were, but you asked him to mark the Bristol Hotel. That's what he did on the map. Perhaps during the next break, you could inform me whether there's any better source, because, well, the examining of a witness is finally under my control, and I will not allow, as you may have noticed before - I don't know whether it's true or not in this case - but I will not allow any misrepresentation of earlier testimony to another witness. But if you find a better source, I'd be glad to accept that I was wrong. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in order to avoid this confusion, I will ask the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you know -- or I will ask the question if he knows if those buildings were on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the front line was Miljacka.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I'll then withdraw my question with regards to whether he knows if the military or the army was stationed in those buildings. My question was in fact the following, if he knew, according to Witness Sabljica, if he knew that those buildings were on the front line?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I already answered that the front line was along the Miljacka River, so Miljacka didn't belong to anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, then, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, do you have any additional questions? Because that's the last thing you indicated that would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you. I would just like to clarify one point. I would like to ask the Chamber, however, when does the Chamber wish to take the next break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Normally, we would have a break after seven minutes from now. So if you would -- if it's just one point you want to clarify, that if you could do it in seven minutes, would be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid, Mr. President, it might take just a bit more, and I also had a technical problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's start and see where we come.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had a technical problem in the meantime. My computer that I closed is not operational any more, unfortunately. So I would like to ask you, then, to be kind enough to allow me to perhaps call a technician right now if we have a break. Right now, I will then ask the technician to come and to see what happened to my screen, or if you want me, I can ask questions by memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the Livenote computer?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm under the impression that it's not only the Livenote but also the transcript itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, usually I connect it by, of course, choosing Livenote, then open the file which is the case, that's the Galic file, then open the transcript. But if a technician could assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, however, I believe Mr. President, I tried so much today. I have a real problem right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll ask the technician to assist you and perhaps meanwhile we could continue -- or do you need the computer for your questioning?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We never know what the future reserves to us. This is why I would prefer to have this tool.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break for 20 minutes until a quarter to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I hope that the technical problems have been solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. Regarding the laptop, it couldn't be fixed, but I will be working on the other screen, on another laptop, hoping that that will not affect anyone. May I continue, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I remind you that -- well, if you would stick very strictly to the time used by the Prosecution, that you have five minutes left. Would you please keep that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for reminding me, Mr. President. But I'm asked to speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, good afternoon. Would you please give me the name, first name, and the date of birth of the first person killed, if you could, and loudly, then of the second. Witness, we only have five minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution objects. The question is not quite clear. The first person killed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you asked for the first person killed. You mean in The Hague this year or in the fire brigade or -- perhaps it would be wise to very precise in questioning instead of reminding the witness that you've only got five minutes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This witness stated here before you that there were people assassinated in their sleep, murdered in their sleep. So I want to know who it was and I want the name of the first person killed in his sleep, his first and last name, age, and place of birth. It is very important. Because if that is the truth that he has said, it is your duty, perhaps, to start an investigation on the basis of what the witness has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So Witness, I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please answer the question. You referred Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to people that would be killed in their sleep. I think it had something to do with military -- young. I could try to find the place, but you testified about people that would be killed during their sleep. Do you know their names? Please answer the question, then.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the names, but I attended their funerals at Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you went to the funerals of people whose name you don't even know. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were recruits, Muslims, who were killed in the JNA in their sleep, and this happened throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So you went to attend a funeral, an important event, and you can't tell me a single name, a single first name now in this courtroom before this Chamber? Not a single name, Witness? Not a single little name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- would you please use your five minutes as you should do it. Small name, big name. The witness has testified clearly that he attended a funeral of one or more persons - I do not know - of who he doesn't know the name. It's of no use to question the way you continued. Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Quite, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, give me the name, please, of the firefighters who shelled the city, and you used the plural.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. I'm not aware of the witness testifying about any firefighters who shelled the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could you please indicate the place where the witness said the firefighters -- or is it a translation problem, Mr. Piletta-Zanin? I didn't follow the French text.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I refer to the English transcript, page 13 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are referring to what line?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 13, 13, and 13.14. I think there's no possible confusion. [In English] "Who had left, they had also shelled us, and they have also shelled our fire station."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the question -- the question is whether you could give the name of firefighters that left your department of which you stated -- you testified that they shelled you and shelled your fire station.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: When I said that 67 firefighters, Serbs, left the fire brigade and went, therefore, to join the Serb forces that shelled us, then I confirm, for instance, Mico Cicovic, who was later killed at Zepa. He lives at Pale. Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'll stop you there, Witness. What evidence can you give us to prove that this particular man was behind a gun and that he launched projectiles on Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first ask you, Mr. Jusufovic. When you said that the people who left you were those who shelled you later on, did you mean to say that those individuals were individually participating in the shelling of the city, or did you mean to say that those who left your department later on belonged to the other side of the conflict and the other party in the conflict shelled Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I was thinking of this latter case, that they joined the other side, the side that shelled Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President. Thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So, Witness, you cannot assert in this Chamber that former Serb firefighters actually operated any weapon to shell you. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see them shelling, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. When I'm cross-examining you, l should like you to limit yourself to what you saw and knew. I come back to those people who were allegedly killed in their sleep. In which barracks was that and when?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you understood me correctly. This was in 1991 when there was the war in Croatia. We weren't talking at all about this period covered by the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But you yourself spoke about it, not me. Why did you speak about it, then, if you knew the period covered by the indictment? Why did you mention it?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Because the question was of what -- what ethnicity was represented in the former JNA. And then I answered that there were very few Muslims for this reason. That's the period of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you were speaking about the period covered by the indictment. How do you know that period? How do you know what period the indictment covers?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I know that it is from the 7th of September, 1992, until August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I didn't ask you what you know; I asked you how did you know that and what is the source of your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I know that before, that all the commanders in command of the siege of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you spoke about the period covered by the indictment. How did you know which was the period covered by the indictment, which implies that you have a knowledge of the indictment? How do you know that, that you're familiar with the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I lived in Sarajevo, and I know all the commanders who were around Sarajevo. I know that General Galic in that period was the commander of the encirclement of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, how do you know the period covered by the indictment? I'm not talking about the period when General Galic may have been in Sarajevo. You used this term yourself, "the period covered by the indictment." Who informed you about that?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I knew it, and probably I was informed. I asked the Prosecution, the people I talked to, probably. When I was collecting information about interventions, I asked which period they were interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You mean, Witness, that when you were collecting your statistical data, you provided them upon request, upon request, I'm saying that, as required?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Throughout the war, there need not be a request. We collect information. We have these intervention forms. And when they came to talk to me in connection with fire extinguishing and how things were, I presented all the information for the whole period of the war. And then they told me it was for General Galic's trial, for such and such a period.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. So you're confirming now that you did not provide documents upon the request of anyone at all and tailored to a request.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand what you're asking me, but let me clarify: The fire brigade has information for the whole war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Let me make my question much clearer. I'm asking you whether you produced documents to cover a certain period at the request, for example, of the Prosecution. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Which documents did you produce?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The intervention forms, collective data.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, then, that these documents were compiled proforma and, therefore, at the request of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The documents were certainly anyway collected. Even if I had never come to this Court, they exist, the data that exists, and I spoke to several officials of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'd like to show the witness a document, with your permission and with the assistance of the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. May I remind you that I said I would strictly keep you to the time. You would have five minutes. Would you please use your time efficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall try and be as efficient as possible, and I think I'll succeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I'm going to show you a document. While the usher is distributing it to all the parties, I would like to know whether you recognise this document as coming from your service. It is Document 0020-5173, the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- could have prenumbered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have a copy, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any copies for the interpreters?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think they will need it, but we do have copies for the booths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll wait a few moments for the distribution to the booths. I'm sure it will be done very quickly. Thank you very much, usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document as emanating from your service?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I see my signature on it, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, could you indicate the date of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. There's no date on it. But obviously I see it covers the period up to 1994 only.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. I'm simply going to read, and I thank the booth for following me. I'm just going to read the first sentence of the text to be found on page 3, and I will have a question after that about it. And I'm reading, I'm quoting: "In the period from the 5th of April, 1992 until the 10th of August, 1994, the brigade had a total of 1.065 interventions." Witness, when you look at this date, the 10th of August, 1994, why did you indicate that date on this document?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know the reasons why this document was compiled, but there were also bulletins that were issued. And in those bulletins there are the names of the killed and wounded firefighters. We were collecting that kind of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, Witness. What is the number of interventions that I read at the bottom of this list? Is it correct to say 120? Do you see, like me, that the number indicated is 120, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you please turn to page 1 of that document. So it is a list of interventions that your brigade did, and you signed it, though there is no date. Will you read what it says under "3," ordinal number 3. Would you read it out, please, number 3.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: MUP motel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What does MUP mean, Witness?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Exactly. You said under oath in this Chamber that you never saw any military activities, any soldiers, when you went to extinguish fires. And when you went to this MUP building, you didn't see any soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't go there. You know that until the end of May, I was not a firefighter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would you please refrain from reminding the witness that he's under oath. If it's necessary, you can address me. I told you this before. I'd like you to keep this in mind. Especially I waited until the answer was given. And the explanation of the witness clearly indicates that it was not the moment to remind him that he was under oath. This is not a debating club, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'm trying to understand things that are escaping me apparently, so I'll have another question under point 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You have another indication. Will you read it out loud, please.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: "MU building Vratza."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Where is Vratza?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Above Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you have this MUP, is that again the Ministry of the Interior, the same ministry?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is a school, the police school, police academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, were these targets of a civilian nature, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: There were children of 15 in that facility going to school, and again, that is the same date, the 10th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I have taken note of your answer. But the establishment itself, you were telling us that children were not going to school any more. But the establishment itself, was it a civilian target?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: On the 10th of April, that had still not been conquered. Children were going to school. People who complete elementary school enroll at the secondary level police academy. And it was attacked - I don't know why - and it burnt down. There was a fire there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry for taking up time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But I'm asking you whether MUP is, according to you, a civilian target. Could you please answer that question for me?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: You have to understand that children were not policemen. This was a secondary school that they are training to become policemen in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, the MUP headquarters, the motel, MUP motel, is that a civilian object or not, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It perhaps was not a civilian target. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Witness, in this list you mention a certain number of other places where, during the 120 interventions took place, because of fires. We have the Loris building. What could you tell us regarding the Centrotrans garage?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you're interested in. I didn't take part in those interventions. But I know that my Stup commander, Mehmedalija, was wounded there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What I'm interested in is what you know about this garage. What was there in that garage? What was in that garage?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: If you are referring to the intervention that I have in mind, there were several interventions. But there were Centrotrans buses there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Those buses, were they used by the army?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me the date of that intervention, and then I'll be able to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: 31st July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I think those buses by then no longer existed. They had already been shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But those buses before, were they used by the army?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: That was the beginning of the war. I don't even know that there was an army. We were not an armed force. We didn't have an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Until when did you remain a militia force?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Until the beginning of June, maybe the end of May. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: June of which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I just talked to you about the end of July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm telling you that I don't know. I don't know during that intervention who used the buses. I don't even know if everything was shelled at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, in that list comprised of 120 names, are there any locations that could have been in Nedzarici during the fire that you mentioned earlier, and if so, where?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what fire you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: In answer to a question of my learned friend earlier, you talked about a voluntary fire that was put out because there was a -- explosives in that list of 120 interventions.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the question. The interpreter didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I know that we did not put out the fire in Nedzarici, and I heard that for the first time from your colleague, the mention of this city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see that the interpretation asked for the question to be repeated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will ask this question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, on the list that you have before you, is there one installation that would refer to this fire that occurred on Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for your intervention. I was not following the transcript that is behind me.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will answer again. Regarding this intervention, I don't know anything of it. I heard for the first time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer, Witness. I would like to go back to some of your statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you indicated to us that you would need approximately, I think you were talking about some 10 minutes, and you had a technical problem as well. You've taken now 35 minutes. You did not use all these 35 minutes in a way which could be qualified as efficient. You get another 5 minutes. If you say -- you are putting your next question, yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, are you an expert witness with regards to ballistics, yes Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. or no?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, did you follow courses when it comes to strategic matters, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: How were you able to confirm, therefore, that you know what the target was which civilians shelled [sic] because you said that you were not a strategic expert? Did you know what was the objective of the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I knew -- I told you that this was my opinion, because we had a school. Now, I don't know what happened to the other cities that could not defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: It does not say in the transcript that you said that it is your own opinion. I will now take note of the fact that it is your own opinion and not the reflection of truth. How can you know with certainty that it was Serbs who were shelling you? And I am talking in absolutely general terms. If you're not the ballistic expert and you cannot know where the shots came from, how would you know then?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I am not a ballistics' expert but we knew who was on the hills and we also knew who would call us on the radio to tell us we are going to send you five shells right now, which actually arrived and landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: According to you, Witness, who shelled Markale?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: How can you confirm this? How can you claim this?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Because they were shelling all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And you claim this as a witness today?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do claim this as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Mr. Mundis, any need to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, you still have before you Defence Exhibit 83; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: 82. Can you read for the benefit of the Trial Chamber the heading at the top of page 1 of that document.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: "Fires on buildings of special importance that occurred from the aggressors' shelling and other weapons."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now again, turn if you would, please, to page 3 of this document. There's a reference there to "1.065 interventions" during the dates indicated on that document. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And it's your testimony that the 120 incidents listed on this document are simply a subset of that 1.065 interventions?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention now to the diary of Stjepan Siber that Ms. Pilipovic read a portion to you of. Have you ever met Mr. Siber?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever provide him with any information that he then incorporated in his diary?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did any of your colleagues, friends, co-workers, neighbours, family members, et cetera, ever tell you that they had spoken to this author?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you have any opinion or any information as to the source of the material that was read to you from that book this morning?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: No, I do not. It's very strange because on that date, I had been working there for two months. I was a commander for only two months at that point, and I am very surprised that somebody could say something like this for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnicity of Stjepan Siber?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know that he is Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jusufovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Prosecution has no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jusufovic, I have only a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first one is, you testified that while you tried to use the, as you called them, firing steps mounted on vehicles, that you were sniped at and that for that reason you couldn't use them any more. When you tried to do this, do you remember what kind of building you're trying -- on what kind of building you're trying to extinguish a fire, or perhaps even if you would remember the building, what building it was?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It was the building of the PTT and the building that we saw on the videoclip earlier called the matchbox.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you try to use it only once or did you try it several times?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Twice on that occasion, because on both times, they were shooting at us, so we couldn't dare any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I'm interested to know is whether the other building was an apartment block or an office building or what kind of building it was.

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It was the tallest high-rise apartment building in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With apartments where people lived or offices or...

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: It was an apartment building. We call it the matchbox because there are a lot of apartments, workers' apartments in that building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much for that answer. Then you answered a question about the Markale market. Do you have any personal knowledge that you ever had to do with the Markale market shelling incident on an official level?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the only thing we had to do was to wash out the blood after the event. That is all. We couldn't do anything else there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you said the source of your knowledge was that you were always shelled by the Serbian army. Does this indicate that your opinion that it was the Serb army that shelled you was based just on your general experience?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. From my personal experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. Mr. Jusufovic, this ends your examination as a witness, unless -- I see that Ms. Pilipovic has still perhaps an additional question in relation to one of the questions --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed. I was a bit too quick.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The questions that you just asked, so I have one question stemming from those questions. In what part of the town was the building called the matchbox?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: The social.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Where is it, in what part of the town?

utterances.speaker: MESUD JUSUFOVIC
utterances.text: Dolatz Malta.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: After having answered this last question, Mr. Jusufovic, I know it's a very long way to come to The Hague and to testify. And we thank you very much for coming to The Hague, for answering all the questions, of course, the questions and your answers being important for all of us in this courtroom to perform our tasks, and especially for the Court to prepare decisions we'll have to take. So thank you very much for coming, and I wish you a safe journey home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please lead Mr. Jusufovic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you please assist us. We saw a video, but that has been played before and it's already known. New documents, Madam Registrar. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The registrar can correct me if I am wrong, Mr. President, but I believe the video previously was simply marked for identification which is why we had given it the number P3609.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I believe it was marked for identification number 8 previously.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document marked for identification number 8 is a DVD containing various clips, so perhaps that clip was included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you now tender the video in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And apart from that, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P3609, the video. D83, the three-page document signed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the reference to 82 in the transcript was not correct, it's finally 83. Both are admitted in evidence. Mr. Mundis, I see --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp will take the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp. Yes, we have still almost a quarter of an hour, so I'd like to start, Mr. Stamp. I just hope that the usher will bring the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlic - I assume that you're Mr. Fazlic - before giving testimony in this Court, the Rules require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. I invite you to make that declaration, and the text has just been handed out to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Fazlic, I'll have to tell you that it will not be very long today that you'll be examined, but we'll then continue tomorrow because we only have a session in the morning hours. But you'll first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you start by stating your name, please.

utterances.speaker: ISMET FAZLIC
utterances.text: My name is Ismet Fazlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you live in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ISMET FAZLIC
utterances.text: I live in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you presently employed?

utterances.speaker: ISMET FAZLIC
utterances.text: No. I'm an invalid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: To what extent are you an invalid?

utterances.speaker: ISMET FAZLIC
utterances.text: I am 70 per cent disabled.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, how long have you lived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ISMET FAZLIC
utterances.text: I was born in Sarajevo, and I have been living there for 46 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And did you live there in the period between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: ISMET FAZLIC
utterances.text: Yes. On Dobrinja, in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, before that period, and that is a period of the conflict of the early 1990s, did you work?

utterances.speaker: ISMET FAZLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What type of employment were you involved in?

utterances.speaker: ISMET FAZLIC
utterances.text: I was a highly skilled worker for central heating, and I was working in a company called Upi in Jusovici.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And during the period of the conflict up until approximately June 1993, were you in any way employed?

utterances.speaker: ISMET FAZLIC
utterances.text: No. Since Dobrinja was under blockade, we could not leave Dobrinja for six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, in that period, up until June 1993, were you engaged in any type of activity?

utterances.speaker: ISMET FAZLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was working as a civilian in the civilian defence of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, can you recall the 1st of June, 1993? Were you in Dobrinja that day?

utterances.speaker: ISMET FAZLIC
utterances.text: On the 1st of June, 1993, I was injured, wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And in which area, in which district were you injured? Was it in Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: ISMET FAZLIC
utterances.text: I was wounded in Dobrinja during a football match. It took place on the 1st of June, 1992. I was the referee for a football match.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was this football match the 1st of June 1993 or the 1st of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: ISMET FAZLIC
utterances.text: It was on the 1st of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, how was this football match organised? Can you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: ISMET FAZLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. As of the beginning of the siege of Sarajevo and of Dobrinja, we lived in the ground, in basements. And then in order to leave the grounds to come outside, we thought that it would do us good. So we organised a football match because youth, as any youth in the world, wished to relax a little bit, to have a taste of freedom. And because it was a beautiful day, the weather was nice, there was no shooting on that day, it was a calm day, we had organised a football match comprised of 12 teams with five players each, and each of these players was to give a box of cigarettes. And then the winner would go to Skenderija to play a football tournament.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Now, what time was this football tournament arranged to begin that day?

utterances.speaker: ISMET FAZLIC
utterances.text: The tournament began at 9.00. The first football match for which Enver Sabanhadzovic was a referee finished. However, when the second match started, I was the referee for that particular match --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the organisation of this football tournament coincident with any particular holiday period?

utterances.speaker: ISMET FAZLIC
utterances.text: Yes. It corresponded with the Muslim Korban Bajram, but it was not a religious event because everybody participated in that match, everybody who lived in the territory of Dobrinja, Anto, Salko, Ismet, Marko, everybody who wanted could have participated. We all took part in this game. And Marko and Dragan and Damir and lots of them were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you say "lots of them" and "everybody participated," who are you referring to? Are you saying that all the ethnicities that lived in Dobrinja at the time participated in the tournament?

utterances.speaker: ISMET FAZLIC
utterances.text: Yes. And today also. It's a multi-ethnic neighbourhood, and people as people live in Dobrinja. They all live side by side without any problems. People, Serbian, Croats, Muslims, gypsies, everybody who had an apartment in Dobrinja, they all lived there, and nobody was touched during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you took us to the second game in the tournament when you were the referee. At about what time did that second game begin?

utterances.speaker: ISMET FAZLIC
utterances.text: The second game started around 10.00 in the morning and lasted until 10 -- after 10.00, about 20 minutes maybe, more or less. And around 10 after 10.00, the first shell fell, landed between us and did what it did. And the second shell landed only 10 metres behind, behind some cars, and it just injured one man.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Fazlic. We'll get to that part of it in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't know, Mr. President, if it's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think we could have gone for five minutes, but if you say it's better to -- also because the witness is only a few minutes in this courtroom, and it might give him a more comfortable feeling that it was not just for a split second that he was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm guided, Mr. President. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said two shells landed. But before we get to that, could you just briefly describe the place where you had the football game. Where exactly was this?

utterances.speaker: ISMET FAZLIC
utterances.text: We knew what the situation was in Dobrinja. We were looking for the safest possible place and a place where we could secure. We knew where the commandment was of our General Hadzic, and he told us not to gather, not to have these meetings. But however, we did go outside. We took a corner of a parking lot. We hoped that nothing would happen there because it was 15 metres long by 40 metres wide. And there were cars, old cars, that were damaged and they were placed there. So that area was delineated by these cars, old cars.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This area that you selected, was it surrounded by any structures or buildings?
